question: On their way to the giant-king's hall of Utgard, Thor and Loki and the boy Thjalfi spent a stormy night in what they took to be a strange echoing hall with a smaller chamber off one side. At dawn an enormous giant named Skrymir woke nearby, reached down, and picked up the building they had slept in. What had they actually slept inside?
answer: Skrymir's giant glove, with the thumb as the side-room
choices: Skrymir's giant glove, with the thumb as the side-room
Skrymir's wooden travel-chest, lined with bear-fur
A hollow oak Skrymir was carrying as a walking stick
Skrymir's iron drinking-cup, large enough to swim in
context: The story is told in the Prose Edda. Skrymir was an illusion-form of the giant-king Utgard-Loki himself, sent to deceive Thor before the contest in his hall. The three travelers had crept into the 'side-room' for shelter from his thunderous snoring.

question: Thor and his companions Loki and the boy Thjalfi traveled with the giant Skrymir on their way to Utgard. Each night Skrymir's snoring shook the forest. Three separate nights Thor crept over and struck Skrymir's forehead with Mjolnir, blows that should have caved the giant's skull. Each morning Skrymir woke unharmed. What did Skrymir say after the third strike?
answer: Did an acorn just fall on my head from that tree above?
choices: Did an acorn just fall on my head from that tree above?
What was that buzzing on my forehead just now?
These eastern lands have an unusual rain in the night.
Some twigs from the branches have brushed my brow.
context: The giant was actually the disguised illusion of Utgard-Loki, who later confessed that he had set a mountain between himself and Mjolnir. Thor's blows had carved three enormous square valleys into that mountain instead.

question: In the hall of Utgard-Loki, king of the giants, Thor was offered a drinking horn the king's servants said even the smallest of his court could drain in a single pull. Thor took three enormous gulps, deep enough to make his cheeks ache, but the level in the horn barely sank. The king laughed. Once they had left the hall and the illusion was lifted, Utgard-Loki confessed what the horn had truly been connected to. What was at the other end of the horn?
answer: The ocean itself, drawn down by Thor into the first tides
choices: The ocean itself, drawn down by Thor into the first tides
A spring beneath Yggdrasil that no Aesir could drain
The cauldron of Aegir that all the giants drank from
A river running from Mimir's well of wisdom
context: The Prose Edda says the three gulps caused the first tides, ebbing the sea everywhere. Utgard-Loki freely admitted afterward that no one of his court could have drained the horn either; Thor's strength had genuinely terrified him.

question: In the hall of Utgard-Loki, Thor was challenged to a child's game — to lift a great gray cat off the floor. Thor strained, his back muscles cracking, and at last managed to raise one of the cat's paws barely free of the stones. The court laughed. Outside the hall, after the spell broke, Utgard-Loki confessed what the cat had actually been. What was the cat?
answer: Jormungandr, the world-serpent that circles Midgard
choices: Jormungandr, the world-serpent that circles Midgard
Nidhogg, the dragon coiled at Yggdrasil's root
Garm, the hound of Hel chained beneath the world
Fenrir himself, bound and shape-shifted small
context: Utgard-Loki later admitted he had trembled when Thor raised even one paw — he feared the strain would dislodge the serpent from its grip around the world. The challenge was a magical disguise for the world-serpent, Thor's old enemy.

question: Utgard-Loki finally offered Thor one last contest — to wrestle his old foster-nurse, a withered hag named Elli, since none of his warriors would dare grapple the thunder-god. Thor seized her, but the harder he pulled the more solidly she stood. Slowly she forced him down to one knee. The hall laughed. Once Thor had left and the illusion lifted, Utgard-Loki revealed what Elli truly was. Whom had Thor wrestled?
answer: Old age itself, which no creature can ever defeat
choices: Old age itself, which no creature can ever defeat
Death itself, walking among the living as a hag
The Norn Skuld in mortal disguise
Hel's mother Angrboda, the giantess of grief
context: Utgard-Loki confessed afterward that no one had ever beaten Elli — every man and god grows old at last, however strong he begins. Thor's ability to force her to even a knee impressed the giant-king beyond reckoning.

question: At Utgard-Loki's hall the boy Thjalfi, fastest runner Thor had ever known, was challenged to race a small slim youth of the giant-king's court named Hugi. Three times they ran the course; three times Hugi finished so far ahead he was already returning before Thjalfi reached the turning. Once Thor's company left and the spell lifted, the giant-king named what Hugi truly was. Whom had Thjalfi raced?
answer: Thought itself, swifter than any living foot
choices: Thought itself, swifter than any living foot
Wind itself, fleshed as a young man
The runic letter for swiftness given form
A shadow-double cast by the giant-king
context: Hugi means 'Mind' or 'Thought.' Utgard-Loki confessed that Thjalfi was the fastest mortal he had ever seen — but no foot can beat the speed at which a thought races. Thjalfi continued thereafter in Thor's company on many adventures.

question: At Utgard-Loki's hall, Loki boasted he could out-eat any man alive. He was set against one of the king's courtiers, a slim man named Logi, before a long trough piled with roast meat. They ate from opposite ends and met in the middle. Loki had stripped every bone clean. But Logi had eaten the bones AND the trough itself. When the illusion was later lifted, Utgard-Loki revealed Logi's true nature. Whom had Loki competed against?
answer: Wildfire itself, which devours wood and bone alike
choices: Wildfire itself, which devours wood and bone alike
Famine itself, drawn out of Niflheim's mists
A storm-spirit bound into a giant's shape
An iron-jawed troll from Utgard's deep caverns
context: Logi means 'Flame' or 'Wildfire.' Utgard-Loki confessed afterward that he had needed every trick at his disposal to keep Thor's small company from sacking his hall. The Edda's contest-tales are the source of the proverb 'no one beats fire at eating.'

question: Thor came to the hall of the giant Hymir and demanded to go out fishing with him. Hymir laughed and said the boy could come if he brought his own bait. Thor walked across to Hymir's herd of oxen, picked the largest bull (named Himinhrjot, the heaven-bellower), and twisted off its head with his bare hands. He rowed out with Hymir using the ox-head as bait. What was Thor trying to catch?
answer: Jormungandr, the world-serpent coiled around Midgard
choices: Jormungandr, the world-serpent coiled around Midgard
The giant whale Hrosshvalr from the Greenland deeps
Nidhogg the dragon, drawn up from Yggdrasil's root
The kraken-like beast Lyngbakr, the heather-back
context: The Hymir story is told in the Hymiskvitha of the Poetic Edda. Thor had a long enmity with Jormungandr, fated to kill him at Ragnarok. Hymir owned a great brewing cauldron the gods needed — the fishing trip was nominally to feed the household before Thor took the cauldron home.

question: Thor sat in the giant Hymir's boat far out in the deep northern sea, having hooked the world-serpent Jormungandr on his line with an ox-head as bait. The boat planks groaned as Thor braced his feet through the hull and hauled. The serpent's head rose dripping above the gunwale, venom spraying. Hymir went pale with terror, drew his fishing knife, and what did he do?
answer: Cut Thor's line so the serpent fell back into the sea
choices: Cut Thor's line so the serpent fell back into the sea
Threw the ox-head bait into the serpent's open jaws
Stabbed at Thor's hand to make him drop the line
Leaped overboard and swam for the distant shore
context: Thor punched Hymir overboard in fury at his cowardice. The poem records Thor's hammer in his other hand, ready to strike the serpent the moment he drew it close enough. The two were fated to kill each other at Ragnarok instead.

question: Thor sat at the giant Thrym's wedding feast disguised in a bridal veil and Freyja's borrowed gown. Through the gauze Thrym leaned in for a closer look at his new bride and was startled by the burning red eyes glaring back at him. Loki, sitting beside Thor as the bride's quick-witted maid, invented a smooth excuse. What did Loki tell Thrym about the bride's terrible eyes?
answer: She has not slept for eight nights longing for Jotunheim
choices: She has not slept for eight nights longing for Jotunheim
Freyja weeps tears of fire when she is overjoyed
The sun on the road has reddened her eyes through the veil
She has been weeping pearls of joy beneath the linen
context: The story is in the Thrymskvitha of the Poetic Edda. Loki had already invented an explanation for the bride's appetite (Thor ate a whole ox, eight salmon, and three barrels of mead): 'She has not eaten for eight days longing for you.' Both coverups bought time until Mjolnir was placed in the bride's lap to consecrate the marriage.

question: Loki, in one of his cruelest pranks, crept into Thor's hall while the goddess Sif slept and sheared off all of her famously beautiful golden hair, leaving her shorn to the scalp. When Sif woke and the truth came out, Thor seized Loki and threatened to break every bone in his body. What did Loki promise to do to escape Thor's wrath?
answer: Get the dwarfs to forge new hair of real spun gold
choices: Get the dwarfs to forge new hair of real spun gold
Surrender his head as the original wager allowed
Bring back Freyja's necklace as compensation gift
Sail to Niflheim and return with three golden apples
context: Loki went to the Svartalfheim caves and persuaded the sons of Ivaldi to forge the hair, along with the spear Gungnir and the ship Skidbladnir. He then bet his own head that the dwarf brothers Sindri and Brokkr could not equal those treasures — leading to the forging of Mjolnir, Draupnir, and Gullinbursti.

question: Loki stole the goddess Freyja's golden necklace Brisingamen from her sleeping chamber. The watchman of the gods, Heimdall, saw the theft from his post at the rainbow bridge and gave chase across the sea. Loki took the shape of a seal to fight him among the waves and skerries. What shape did Heimdall take to wrestle Loki and recover the necklace?
answer: Heimdall also took seal-shape to fight Loki on the rocks
choices: Heimdall also took seal-shape to fight Loki on the rocks
Heimdall changed to a polar bear and dragged Loki ashore
Heimdall took eagle-form and clawed Loki off the skerry
Heimdall remained in his own form, casting a spell of binding
context: The fight took place on a skerry called Singasteinn. Heimdall recovered the necklace and returned it to Freyja. The episode is referenced in the Husdrapa of the skald Ulfr Uggason and survives in Snorri's Prose Edda.

question: The giant Thiazi, taking the shape of a huge eagle, kidnapped the goddess Idunn from Asgard by trickery — Loki had betrayed her, luring her outside the walls. Once Idunn and her magical apples were gone, the gods began to wither and grow gray. The Aesir gathered Loki in council and demanded he get Idunn back. What did Loki borrow from Freyja to fly to Thiazi's hall of Thrymheim?
answer: Her cloak of falcon feathers, which let any wearer fly
choices: Her cloak of falcon feathers, which let any wearer fly
Her chariot of cats, which could leap from cloud to cloud
Her gold-bristled boar Gullinbursti, who could ride the sky
Her brother Freyr's ship Skidbladnir, which sailed on air
context: Thiazi was Skadi's father. Loki found Idunn alone in the giant's hall while Thiazi was out hunting at sea. He turned Idunn into a nut and flew her back to Asgard in his beak. Thiazi pursued in eagle-form and was burned to death when the gods lit the shavings of Asgard's walls as he overflew.

question: Loki, Odin, and Hoenir traveled through Jotunheim and tried to roast an ox for supper, but no matter how long the fire burned the meat stayed raw. An enormous eagle in a nearby tree called down — give me the best portion and your fire will cook. The eagle was the giant Thiazi in disguise. When Loki angrily struck the eagle with a long pole, what happened to him?
answer: He stuck fast to the pole, and the eagle flew off carrying him
choices: He stuck fast to the pole, and the eagle flew off carrying him
The pole transformed in his hand into a long snake
He was lifted into the tree and pinned among the branches
The eagle vanished in smoke and the ox finally roasted
context: Thiazi dragged Loki through brambles and over crags until Loki begged for mercy. Thiazi demanded that Loki bring the goddess Idunn and her apples out of Asgard as ransom. Loki agreed — and only later, with Freyja's falcon-cloak, undid what he had promised.

question: The giantess Skadi came armored to Asgard seeking vengeance for her father Thiazi, whom the Aesir had killed. To settle her claim peacefully the gods offered her a choice of any Aesir as husband — but she could choose only by looking at his feet beneath a curtain, with the rest of the body hidden. She picked the cleanest, brightest, most graceful pair, hoping they were Balder's. Whose feet had she actually chosen?
answer: Njord's, the old sea-god whose feet were washed white by tides
choices: Njord's, the old sea-god whose feet were washed white by tides
Freyr's, the harvest-god with sun-tanned feet
Tyr's, the war-god with calloused soldier feet
Heimdall's, the bright watcher of the bridge
context: The marriage was unhappy — Skadi loved her mountain home of Thrymheim, Njord loved his coastal hall Noatun. They split nine nights in each. Skadi's other settlement-condition was that the gods make her laugh; that fell to Loki.

question: The giantess Skadi, after killing her father Thiazi, demanded as part of her settlement with the Aesir that they make her laugh — something nobody believed possible in her grief and fury. Loki took up the task himself. He tied one end of a cord to a goat's beard and tied the other end to a sensitive part of his own body. What followed?
answer: Goat and Loki yanked each other shrieking until Skadi laughed
choices: Goat and Loki yanked each other shrieking until Skadi laughed
Loki danced backward on his hands while juggling fire
Loki sang a song mocking every giant in Jotunheim
Loki pulled his eyebrows off and stuck them on a goose
context: The Prose Edda records the scene with a smirk. Skadi laughed at last and the settlement was complete. Odin further completed her satisfaction by taking her father's eyes and placing them in the sky as two stars.

question: The Volsung hero Sigurd was raised by the dwarf-smith Regin, who wanted Sigurd to kill the dragon Fafnir (Regin's brother in dragon-shape) and take the cursed Andvari hoard. Regin first forged Sigurd a new sword which Sigurd shattered on the anvil; then a second, which also broke. At last Sigurd demanded the shards of his father Sigmund's old sword from his mother Hjordis, the broken blade Odin himself had once given Sigmund. What did Sigurd name the reforged sword?
answer: Gram, the sword that split Regin's anvil at the first test
choices: Gram, the sword that split Regin's anvil at the first test
Tyrfing, the cursed sword forged by the dwarfs Dvalin and Durin
Hrunting, the heirloom sword later loaned to the hero Beowulf
Naegling, the ancestor-sword that shattered against the dragon
context: Sigmund had received the sword from Odin himself, who drove it into the Branstock oak at Volsung's hall — only Sigmund could draw it. Reforged from its fragments, Gram was sharp enough to slice a tuft of wool floating downstream. Wagner's 19th-century Ring cycle renamed it Notung in the libretto.

question: The Volsung hero Sigurd, having reforged the sword Gram from his ancestor Sigmund's fragments, rode to the moor where the dragon Fafnir crawled each day to drink at a river. Fafnir's hide was iron-hard above; his belly was the only soft part. Sigurd dug a deep pit in the path the dragon used, climbed down, and waited. What did Sigurd do as Fafnir slithered over the pit?
answer: Stabbed upward into the dragon's heart with Gram
choices: Stabbed upward into the dragon's heart with Gram
Loosed two javelins from below into its throat
Caught its scales as it passed and climbed onto its back
Sprang up and slashed Gram across the dragon's eyes
context: Odin himself, disguised as an old man, had given Sigurd the pit-strategy on the road. Fafnir's blood gushed down into the pit, drenching Sigurd. The dragon spoke as it died, warning that the hoard was cursed — every owner had been slain over it.

question: Balder the Beautiful began dreaming his own death. His mother Frigg traveled the nine worlds extracting a promise from every kind of thing — every metal, every stone, every plant, every disease — that none would ever harm her son. The gods then entertained themselves at feasts by throwing rocks and weapons at Balder, watching them bounce away. The jealous trickster Loki was determined to discover whether Frigg had missed anything. How did he learn she had?
answer: He disguised himself as an old woman and asked Frigg directly
choices: He disguised himself as an old woman and asked Frigg directly
He climbed Yggdrasil and read the runes from its highest branch
He bribed the Norn Skuld with a gift of Andvari's cursed gold
He stole the answer from Mimir's well of memory in seal-shape
context: Frigg admitted to the old woman in conversation that the mistletoe growing west of Valhalla had seemed too young and small to bother asking. Loki took the form of a beggar and went out to cut a sprig. He carved the dart that would end Balder's life and gave it to the blind brother Hodr to throw.

question: Having discovered that the goddess Frigg had skipped a mistletoe sprig in her promises that nothing would harm her son Balder, Loki carved a small dart from the plant. He then approached Balder's blind brother Hodr, who stood mournfully on the edge of the feast where the other gods were merrily throwing things at the invulnerable Balder. What did Loki tell Hodr?
answer: Throw this dart and I will aim your hand at your brother's game
choices: Throw this dart and I will aim your hand at your brother's game
Strike this against the wall and listen to Balder laughing
Take this gift to your brother as a token from the eastern gods
Hold this in your hand and it will speak news of your brother's joy
context: Hodr, eager to take part for once, agreed. Loki guided his hand. The dart struck Balder through and Balder fell dead — the brightest of the gods killed in the middle of a game by his own blind brother's hand. The feast turned to silence.

question: After Balder was killed by Loki's trick with the mistletoe dart, the god Hermod rode Odin's eight-legged horse Sleipnir down to the realm of Hel to plead for his brother's return. Hel agreed on one condition — every living thing in the nine worlds must weep for Balder. The gods sent messengers everywhere. All wept except one giantess in a cave named Tokk. What did Tokk say?
answer: Tokk will weep dry tears, so let Hel hold what she has
choices: Tokk will weep dry tears, so let Hel hold what she has
Tokk has no time for the grief of the Aesir today
Let Frigg weep alone, since I owe her son no tears at all
What good is one giantess against Hel's iron decree?
context: Tokk was Loki himself in disguise. Because of his refusal Balder remained in Hel until after Ragnarok, when he would return to the renewed earth. The gods discovered the deception only later and Loki fled, beginning his pursuit by the Aesir.

question: After Balder's death, the gods finally seized Loki in his hiding-place behind a waterfall. They took him to a cave and brought in his two sons, Vali and Narfi. To bind Loki for eternity they first turned one son against the other. What did the gods do to Vali?
answer: Turned him into a wolf who tore his brother Narfi apart
choices: Turned him into a wolf who tore his brother Narfi apart
Sent him to Hel to swap places with his uncle Balder
Killed him with Gungnir to silence his weeping
Sealed him alive inside the stone of the cave wall
context: Narfi's entrails were then drawn out as the binding cord — and as the gods tightened them around Loki across three sharp stones the entrails turned to iron. Skadi, in vengeance for her father Thiazi, hung a venomous snake above Loki's face. His wife Sigyn stayed beside him with a bowl to catch the venom.

question: After the gods bound Loki across three sharp stones with the iron-hardened entrails of his own son Narfi, the giantess Skadi fastened a venomous serpent in the rocks above his face so that the venom would drip eternally into his eyes. Loki's faithful wife Sigyn refused to leave him. What did she do beside her bound husband?
answer: Held a bowl beneath the snake to catch the dripping venom
choices: Held a bowl beneath the snake to catch the dripping venom
Sang spells of healing to soothe his suffering between drops
Stitched a leather mask across his eyes to shield him
Tried to gnaw through the iron cords with her own teeth
context: Whenever Sigyn turned to empty the full bowl, the venom dripped into Loki's eyes and he convulsed in agony. The Norse said his thrashing was felt across the worlds — the source of earthquakes. He would remain bound until Ragnarok freed him.

question: An unnamed builder came to Asgard offering to wall the city against the jotnar in a single winter, fortified beyond any breach. In return he demanded an extraordinary triple-price. Loki persuaded the wary gods to accept on a tight deadline he thought impossible — first day of summer. What was the builder's asking price for the wall?
answer: The goddess Freyja, plus the sun and the moon
choices: The goddess Freyja, plus the sun and the moon
Odin's spear Gungnir and his eight-legged horse
The apples of Idunn and a place at the Aesir's table
Thor's hammer Mjolnir and Heimdall's golden horn
context: The builder was a giant in disguise. The gods banked on him being unable to finish without help — but his stallion Svadilfari was a working wonder, hauling whole mountains of stone every night. As the deadline closed and the wall neared completion, Loki was sent to make sure the builder lost the bet.

question: When Asgard's mason builder was three days from finishing the colossal wall that would cost the gods Freyja, the sun, and the moon, his stallion Svadilfari was doing most of the heavy hauling. Loki, blamed by the gods for the disastrous deal, had to act. He left the city and met Svadilfari on the night road. What shape did Loki take?
answer: A mare, who whinnied and led the stallion off into the woods
choices: A mare, who whinnied and led the stallion off into the woods
A salmon, blocking the stream the stallion drank from
A great elk who fought Svadilfari off the road by force
A blazing wraith that startled the stallion into a bolt
context: Svadilfari ran after the mare all night and the next day, refusing to return to work. The builder lost the bet by the deadline. He revealed himself as a giant in rage — and Thor, who had been off east fighting trolls, returned in time to smash him with Mjolnir. Loki later returned with an eight-legged foal: Sleipnir.

question: Loki, captured by the giant Geirrod and threatened with death, swore an oath to bring Thor to Geirrod's hall without Mjolnir, without his iron gauntlets, and without his belt of strength. Thor, tricked into going, stopped on the way at the cave of the friendly giantess Grid. What three things did Grid give him to keep him alive at Geirrod's hall?
answer: Her iron gauntlets, an iron belt, and a staff called Gridarvolr
choices: Her iron gauntlets, an iron belt, and a staff called Gridarvolr
Three golden apples for strength, one for each of three days
Three rings, one for sight, one for shielding, one for striking
Three jars of mead, three rune-charms, and a healing comb
context: Grid was the mother of the silent god Vidar. Without her gifts Thor would not have survived the trip — the daughters of Geirrod, the river Vimur, and Geirrod himself all sought to kill him. Loki traveled with Thor under threat.

question: Crossing on foot to the giant Geirrod's hall, leaning on Grid's iron staff Gridarvolr, Thor came to the river Vimur. The water began to rise rapidly under him as he waded — first to his thighs, then to his belly, then to his shoulders. Looking upstream Thor saw what was causing the flood. What did he find?
answer: Geirrod's daughter Gjalp standing astride the river above him
choices: Geirrod's daughter Gjalp standing astride the river above him
Two giant kings damming the river with felled oaks
Jormungandr coiled in the riverbed, swelling the flow
Skadi opening glacier-gates from the upstream mountains
context: Thor picked up a boulder from the riverbed and hurled it at her with such force she fled. He shouted the proverb 'A river must be dammed at its source.' He pulled himself ashore using a rowan tree, which gave the rowan the name 'Thor's rescue.'

question: Thor and Loki at last reached Geirrod's hall. Thor was given the place of honor — a single low chair against the wall. As he sat down he felt the chair rising rapidly toward the ceiling, where the rafters threatened to crush his skull. Bracing Grid's iron staff Gridarvolr above his head, Thor pushed the chair back down with such force that he heard a sharp double crack from underneath it. Whom had he crushed?
answer: Geirrod's daughters Gjalp and Greip, hiding beneath
choices: Geirrod's daughters Gjalp and Greip, hiding beneath
Two ogres planted under the floor of the hall
Two trolls bound under the stones of Geirrod's hearth
Two giant rats Geirrod kept as servants in the wall
context: The double crack was the back of each daughter being broken at once. Geirrod, hearing the sound, knew his trap had failed. He stepped out of his forge with a glowing iron bar caught up in tongs, ready to throw at Thor by another stratagem.

question: After Thor crushed Geirrod's two daughters Gjalp and Greip under the rising chair, the giant himself stepped out of his forge with tongs gripping a glowing iron bar. He whipped the molten iron at Thor across the hall. Thor caught the bar in mid-air with Grid's iron gauntlets and hurled it back. What did the iron do when it struck Geirrod?
answer: Passed through Geirrod, the pillar he hid behind, and the wall
choices: Passed through Geirrod, the pillar he hid behind, and the wall
Lodged in Geirrod's chest and set the giant's beard on fire
Cleaved Geirrod's iron throne in half before striking him
Bounced off the pillar and back into Thor's gauntlet again
context: The story is preserved in the Thorsdrapa by the 10th-century skald Eilif Godrunarson and in Snorri's Prose Edda. The iron passed through all three obstacles and lodged in the hill outside the hall. Thor returned home alive thanks to Grid's three gifts.

question: The sea-giant Aegir held a great feast for all the gods in his hall on Hlesey, brewing ale in the enormous cauldron Thor had once taken from Hymir. Loki had been banished from the feast for killing one of Aegir's servants in jealous rage. He pushed back in anyway and began trading insults around the long benches — every god and goddess in turn. What ended the flyting at last?
answer: Thor's arrival, raising Mjolnir over Loki's head
choices: Thor's arrival, raising Mjolnir over Loki's head
Odin's spear-cast pinning Loki's tongue to the bench
Heimdall blowing Gjallarhorn so loud Loki ran outside
Frigg singing a binding-rune to silence his mouth
context: The Lokasenna of the Poetic Edda preserves the flyting. Loki insulted every god and goddess until Thor returned from an errand east. The trickster fled, hid in a waterfall as a salmon, and was caught with a net the gods themselves were forced to weave from his fishing-knot pattern.

question: After the war between the Aesir and the Vanir ended, the two divine families sealed peace by spitting into a great cauldron. From the spittle the gods shaped a man — Kvasir, the wisest being in the nine worlds, who could answer any question put to him. Two cunning dwarfs named Fjalar and Galar invited Kvasir to a private feast. What did they do to him?
answer: Murdered him and drained his blood into three vessels
choices: Murdered him and drained his blood into three vessels
Imprisoned him in their forge until he taught them every craft
Tricked him into drinking a sleeping-potion lasting a hundred years
Stole his tongue and locked it in an iron chest
context: The dwarfs mixed Kvasir's blood with honey and brewed the Mead of Poetry — any drinker would become a poet or a scholar. They told the Aesir Kvasir had choked on his own wisdom because no one was wise enough to ask the questions that would have saved him.

question: The dwarfs Fjalar and Galar, having brewed the Mead of Poetry from murdered Kvasir's blood mixed with honey, went on to drown the giant Gilling and crush Gilling's wife with a millstone, just for amusement. Gilling's son Suttungr seized the dwarfs and threatened to drown them on a half-tide rock. What price did Suttungr demand for their lives?
answer: The full Mead of Poetry as compensation for his parents
choices: The full Mead of Poetry as compensation for his parents
Their entire treasure-hoard and their forge as well
Their tongues, in payment for words spoken in cruelty
Their service in his hall for a hundred winters
context: Suttungr took the mead home to his mountain Hnitbjorg in Jotunheim, locked it in a deep cave, and set his daughter Gunnlod as its guard. The cave became the source-location for Odin's later theft of the mead, disguised as the farmhand Bolverkr.

question: Determined to win the Mead of Poetry from the giant Suttungr's mountain Hnitbjorg, Odin disguised himself as a farmhand named Bolverkr and tricked Suttungr's brother Baugi into helping him. Baugi produced a magical auger called Rati. What did Odin do at the mountain wall once the auger had drilled through?
answer: Turned himself into a serpent and slipped through the hole
choices: Turned himself into a serpent and slipped through the hole
Crawled in as a beetle and grew large inside the cave
Walked through as smoke and rejoined his shape within
Tore the hole wider with his bare hands and stepped in
context: Baugi tried to stab Odin in the back as he entered, but Odin slithered too fast. Inside the cave Odin found Suttungr's daughter Gunnlod guarding three vats of mead — and persuaded her to give him three sips in exchange for spending three nights with her.

question: After killing the dragon Fafnir and Regin the smith, the Volsung hero Sigurd rode south on his horse Grani and came at last to a great mountain wreathed in flames. He spurred Grani through the wall of fire and found at the top a figure in full armor sleeping deeply on a stone bier. He cut the armor away with the sword Gram. Whom had he found?
answer: Brunhild, the Valkyrie Odin had cursed with sleep
choices: Brunhild, the Valkyrie Odin had cursed with sleep
Gudrun, the king's daughter promised to him by fate
Sigrdrifa, a sea-witch hidden by her father in fire
Skadi the giantess, hiding in mortal disguise
context: Brunhild had defied Odin's order in a battle, choosing to give victory to the wrong king. As punishment Odin pricked her with a sleep-thorn and walled her in fire — only a hero brave enough to ride through the flames could wake her. The story is told in the Volsunga Saga and inspired Wagner's Ring cycle.

question: Having killed the dragon Fafnir and tasted the dragon's blood, the Volsung hero Sigurd suddenly understood the speech of two birds (eagles in some versions) sitting in the branches above him. The birds were warning him about something Regin the dwarf-smith — his foster-father, who had sent him to kill the dragon in the first place — was about to do. What were the birds warning Sigurd about?
answer: Regin was about to murder Sigurd in his sleep for the whole hoard
choices: Regin was about to murder Sigurd in his sleep for the whole hoard
Brunhild the Valkyrie was waiting on a fire-ringed mountain nearby
Odin himself disapproved of Sigurd taking the cursed gold
The dragon's blood would soon turn Sigurd's skin to dragon-scale
context: Sigurd drew Gram and cut off Regin's head before Regin could rise from where he lay nearby. The same birds also told him of the sleeping Valkyrie Brunhild on the fire-ringed mountain. The whole episode is told in the Fafnismal of the Poetic Edda.

question: Thor and the gods needed the enormous cauldron of the giant Hymir for brewing ale at the feast of Aegir. Hymir refused to give it up unless Thor could break a particular drinking-cup of his by sheer strength. Thor hurled it at a stone pillar — the pillar shattered, the cup did not. The giant Hymir's wife whispered to Thor what he must strike the cup against. What did she suggest?
answer: The hardest thing in the hall, which was Hymir's own skull
choices: The hardest thing in the hall, which was Hymir's own skull
The iron anvil set deep in the courtyard floor
The mountain face Hymir had carved his door from
A whetstone Odin had cast away on the threshold
context: Thor flung the cup against Hymir's forehead. The cup shattered; Hymir's brow was undamaged. Thor then heaved the cauldron over his shoulder and walked out. Hymir and a host of giants pursued and were slain by Mjolnir on the way home.

question: After insulting every god at Aegir's feast and fleeing Thor's wrath, Loki hid in a high mountain hut with four doors facing the four winds, so he could watch every approach. The Aesir tracked him through Odin's high seat Hlidskjalf. To escape unseen Loki transformed into a swift salmon and dove into the waterfall pool beneath the hut. How did the gods finally catch him?
answer: They wove a net by copying the burnt pattern of Loki's own work
choices: They wove a net by copying the burnt pattern of Loki's own work
They dragged the pool dry with bronze pails by Heimdall's hand
They sang a fish-spell taught by the sea-giant Aegir himself
They froze the pool solid with Skadi's mountain breath
context: Loki had been the inventor of the fishing-net. He burned his draft pattern in the hearth before fleeing, but Kvasir (in some versions, or a wise Aesir) saw the ashy outline. They wove a copy and trapped him. As Loki tried to leap clear, Thor caught him by the tail — and Loki's tail has been narrow ever since for all his salmon-kin.

question: After Loki's mare-trick lured away the giant builder's stallion Svadilfari, the builder of Asgard's wall came up three days short of the deadline he had bet on. In rage at being cheated of his prize (Freyja, plus the sun and the moon), the builder threw off his disguise and revealed himself as a frost giant. What happened next?
answer: Thor returned from the east and crushed his skull with Mjolnir
choices: Thor returned from the east and crushed his skull with Mjolnir
Tyr fought him hand to hand and threw him from the wall
Odin pinned him to the new stone with the spear Gungnir
Heimdall blew Gjallarhorn and the giant fled into Jotunheim
context: The Aesir broke their sworn oath in killing the builder — a deception they justified because the builder had broken his oath by being a giant in disguise. The wall stood completed. Loki would later bear Sleipnir, the eight-legged foal, the son of Svadilfari.

question: Months after the builder of Asgard's wall had been killed by Thor, Loki returned to Asgard leading a strange foal he had borne while in mare-shape. The colt had eight legs and could outrun any horse alive. Loki presented the foal as a gift. Whom did Loki give the eight-legged horse to?
answer: Odin, who made Sleipnir his own mount forever after
choices: Odin, who made Sleipnir his own mount forever after
Thor, who could not be carried by ordinary horses
Tyr, as compensation for the hand Fenrir had bitten off
Hermod, who rode the world as a messenger of the gods
context: Sleipnir could gallop across sea and sky and travel between worlds — including down to Hel itself, which Hermod did on him after Balder's death. The eight legs made Sleipnir the fastest horse in the nine worlds. Odin and Sleipnir are depicted together on the Tjängvide image-stone from Gotland (8th century).

question: The Volsung hero Sigurd, after killing the dragon Fafnir with his ancestor's reforged sword Gram, paused at Fafnir's hoard to load Grani his horse with as much gold as the beast could carry. Among the treasure lay a magical helm and a coat of mail. What did the dying Fafnir warn Sigurd as the dragon's life went out?
answer: The hoard is cursed, and every owner will be slain over it
choices: The hoard is cursed, and every owner will be slain over it
Regin will kill you tonight unless you strike him first
Brunhild waits on a fire-ringed mountain bearing your name
Odin himself will demand the gold before Ragnarok comes
context: Fafnir's warning came true. Sigurd was murdered in his sleep by his brother-in-law Guttorm. Brunhild, who loved Sigurd, killed herself on his pyre. The hoard passed to the Burgundian kings and brought destruction to their entire line. The Volsunga Saga is the source of Wagner's Ring of the Nibelung.

question: Setting out to reach the hall of the giant-king Utgard-Loki, Thor took with him his servant Thjalfi and Loki the trickster. They met an enormous giant named Skrymir who agreed to travel with them. That night Thor and his companions camped beside Skrymir's snoring, which shook the forest. While Skrymir slept, Thor crept over and struck him on the forehead with Mjolnir — a blow that should have caved any skull. Skrymir half-opened one eye. Twice more during the night Thor struck him, the third time with all his strength. Each time Skrymir woke a little and rolled over. What did the giant ask Thor at dawn?
answer: Whether some twigs and acorns had fallen on his head in the night
choices: Whether some twigs and acorns had fallen on his head in the night
Whether a small bear had been sniffing about the camp
Whether Thor had heard the strange thumping from beyond the river
Whether the night-wind had brought rain across his face
context: Skrymir was an illusion-form sent by Utgard-Loki. The giant later confessed that he had placed a mountain invisibly between his forehead and Mjolnir. Thor's three blows had carved three enormous square valleys into that mountain — but not into the giant's brow. The Prose Edda makes the deception the prelude to the contests in Utgard's hall.

question: At Utgard-Loki's hall Thor and his companions failed five contests — Loki could not outeat the courtier Logi at a meat-trough; Thjalfi could not outrun the youth Hugi; Thor could not drain a drinking horn nor lift a great gray cat from the floor; and Thor could not wrestle down the king's old foster-nurse Elli. Their party left ashamed. Once well outside the city, Utgard-Loki overtook them on the road and confessed the contests had been magical disguises. He named what each opponent had truly been. Which set is correct?
answer: Logi = wildfire, Hugi = thought, horn = the sea, cat = Jormungandr, Elli = old age
choices: Logi = wildfire, Hugi = thought, horn = the sea, cat = Jormungandr, Elli = old age
Logi = lightning, Hugi = wind, horn = a glacier, cat = Garm, Elli = grief
Logi = a salamander, Hugi = a hawk, horn = Mimir's well, cat = Nidhogg, Elli = sorrow
Logi = a furnace, Hugi = a falcon, horn = a fjord, cat = Geri, Elli = winter
context: Utgard-Loki said even Thor's near-misses had terrified him — three gulps had pulled the sea down to its first tides; lifting one of the cat's paws had nearly dislodged Jormungandr from his world-grip; pressing Elli to a single knee was further than any creature had ever managed against old age itself. The giant-king vanished as Thor reached for Mjolnir, and Utgard's hall went with him.

question: Thor walked far north to the hall of the giant Hymir to fetch a brewing cauldron for the gods. Hymir laughed at the boy and said he could fish with him only if he brought his own bait. Thor strode over to Hymir's herd, picked the largest of the giant's oxen — a bull named Himinhrjot, the heaven-bellower — and twisted off its head with his bare hands. The two rowed far past Hymir's usual grounds. Thor baited his hook with the ox-head, cast the line into the deepest water, and pulled. The line went rigid and the boat-planks cracked under Thor's straining feet. What was on the other end of his line?
answer: Jormungandr, the venom-spraying world-serpent of Midgard
choices: Jormungandr, the venom-spraying world-serpent of Midgard
The dragon Nidhogg from beneath Yggdrasil's root
The whale Hrosshvalr from the Greenland deep
The kraken-like Lyngbakr, the false heather-back
context: The Hymiskvitha of the Poetic Edda preserves the trip. The serpent's head rose dripping above the gunwale, venom spraying. Thor lifted Mjolnir to strike — and at that moment Hymir, terrified, drew his fishing knife and cut Thor's line. The serpent sank back into the sea. The two are fated to kill each other at Ragnarok.

question: Thor woke one morning to find Mjolnir gone. The giant Thrym had stolen it, hidden it eight miles under the earth, and would return it only in exchange for the goddess Freyja as bride. Freyja refused. Heimdall proposed instead that Thor go himself disguised in Freyja's bridal gown and golden necklace, with Loki as the bride's maid. At the wedding feast in Thrym's hall, Thor ate an entire ox, eight salmon, and three barrels of mead in one sitting. The giant Thrym pulled back the veil for a closer look — and was startled by the red eyes glaring through. What did Loki tell Thrym to explain the appetite and the burning eyes?
answer: She has not slept or eaten for eight nights longing for Jotunheim
choices: She has not slept or eaten for eight nights longing for Jotunheim
Freyja eats fire when she rejoices and weeps tears of ember
The Aesir's mead has reddened her cheeks before the ceremony
She has been weeping pearls of joy beneath the linen veil
context: When the small hammer was brought out to consecrate the marriage and placed in the bride's lap, Thor seized it. The story is in the Thrymskvitha of the Poetic Edda. Thor killed Thrym first, then every giant in the hall, then Thrym's elderly mother who had begged a bride-gift. He returned to Asgard with Mjolnir.

question: After Loki sheared Sif's golden hair while she slept, Thor seized him by the throat and threatened to break every bone in his body. Loki swore he would replace the hair with real gold from the dwarfs. He went down to Svartalfheim, where the sons of Ivaldi forged three treasures — Sif's new hair of spun gold, the spear Gungnir, and the ship Skidbladnir. Loki then bet his own head with two more dwarfs, Sindri and Brokkr, that they could not forge three treasures as fine. Brokkr blew the bellows while Sindri worked. What were the three treasures Sindri and Brokkr made?
answer: The hammer Mjolnir, the ring Draupnir, and the boar Gullinbursti
choices: The hammer Mjolnir, the ring Draupnir, and the boar Gullinbursti
The horse Sleipnir, the necklace Brisingamen, and the horn Gjallarhorn
The sword Gram, the cloak of falcon feathers, and the apples of Idunn
The cauldron of Aegir, the iron belt Megingjord, and the bow of Ullr
context: Loki, desperate to save his head, took the shape of a biting fly and bit Brokkr's eyelid as Sindri was forging Mjolnir. Brokkr flinched at the bellows-bellows and the hammer's handle came out short. The Aesir judged Mjolnir the finest of the six treasures despite the short handle. Loki kept his head only by arguing that his neck (which had not been wagered) could not be cut.

question: Loki lost the dwarfs' wager when the Aesir judged Mjolnir the finest of the six treasures forged for the gods. The dwarf Brokkr came forward to claim Loki's head — but Loki argued that nobody had wagered his neck, which the dwarf would have to cut to take the head. Brokkr was furious but the Aesir backed Loki's lawyering. Brokkr then took an awl and a leather thong and did something different to Loki's head instead. What did Brokkr do?
answer: Stitched Loki's lips together with the awl and the thong
choices: Stitched Loki's lips together with the awl and the thong
Branded a runic curse on the back of his bald skull
Pulled out three teeth as substitute for the head debt
Hammered the awl through both his ears as a slave's mark
context: The wound was called Vartari. Loki tore the thong out as soon as Brokkr left, leaving him scarred at the lips ever after. The Prose Edda's Skaldskaparmal preserves the whole story — the six treasures, the wager, the fly, the legal argument, the stitching.

question: Traveling through Jotunheim with Odin and Hoenir, Loki was stuck fast to a long pole by the giant Thiazi (in eagle-form). Thiazi flew off with him, dragged him through brambles and over crags, and threatened to never let go unless Loki swore an oath. What did Loki swear to do?
answer: Lure Idunn and her apples of youth out of Asgard so Thiazi could seize her
choices: Lure Idunn and her apples of youth out of Asgard so Thiazi could seize her
Hand over Thor's hammer Mjolnir to Thiazi at the next dawn
Steal Freyja's necklace Brisingamen from her sleeping chamber
Open the gate of Asgard at midnight for the frost giants
context: Loki carried out his oath under coercion. He told Idunn he had found an orchard outside Asgard with apples better than her own and persuaded her to bring hers for comparison. Thiazi swept down and carried her off to his hall Thrymheim. The Aesir, deprived of Idunn's apples, began withering and turning gray.

question: When the giant Thiazi had carried off Idunn and her apples, the Aesir began aging rapidly. They threatened Loki with death unless he brought her back. Loki borrowed Freyja's cloak of falcon-feathers and flew to Thrymheim. Finding Idunn alone (Thiazi was out at sea), Loki transformed her into a nut and flew home in his beak. Thiazi returned, found her gone, took eagle-shape and pursued. The Aesir saw the falcon and the great eagle coming and prepared. What did they do as the eagle crossed the wall?
answer: Lit wood shavings on the wall so Thiazi's wings caught fire
choices: Lit wood shavings on the wall so Thiazi's wings caught fire
Pulled the gates closed and Thiazi smashed against them senseless
Heimdall blew Gjallarhorn so loud Thiazi tumbled stunned to earth
Thor swung Mjolnir and shattered the eagle in a single blow
context: Thiazi fell inside Asgard's wall and was killed by the gods. Odin took the giant's eyes and placed them in the sky as two stars. Thiazi's armed daughter Skadi later came to Asgard demanding vengeance — leading to her marriage to Njord by feet alone, and Loki's antics with a goat to make her laugh.

question: The giantess Skadi, armed in steel from helm to greaves, came to Asgard demanding compensation for her father Thiazi's death. The Aesir offered to settle the blood-feud in three steps. First, Odin took her father's eyes and placed them in the sky as two stars. Second, she could choose any unmarried Aesir as husband — but only by looking at their feet beneath a long curtain. Third, somebody had to make her laugh, which seemed impossible in her grief. She chose by feet alone, picked the brightest pair hoping for Baldur, and got Njord. Who finally made her laugh, and how?
answer: Loki, by tying a cord between his groin and a goat's beard
choices: Loki, by tying a cord between his groin and a goat's beard
Bragi, by reciting a poem about Skadi as a heroic Valkyrie
Thor, by juggling Mjolnir over his head while doing handstands
Heimdall, by playing his great horn Gjallarhorn at full blast
context: Loki shrieked and the goat shrieked back and both pulled and twisted at one another until Loki fell into Skadi's lap. She laughed, and the settlement was done. The marriage of Skadi and Njord did not last — she loved mountains and wolf-howl, he loved coasts and gull-cry; they split nine nights in each but soon lived apart.

question: The Volsung hero Sigurd was the son of Sigmund (slain in battle) and was raised by the dwarf-smith Regin in the court of King Hjalprek. Regin wanted Sigurd to kill the dragon Fafnir — Regin's own brother, who had taken dragon-shape to hoard the cursed Andvari gold. Regin forged Sigurd two swords, both of which Sigurd shattered on the anvil to prove their weakness. At last Sigurd demanded the fragments of his father's old sword from his mother Hjordis — a blade Odin himself had once driven into the Branstock oak at Volsung's hall. What did Sigurd's reforged sword do to Regin's anvil?
answer: Split the anvil clean in two with a single downward stroke
choices: Split the anvil clean in two with a single downward stroke
Glowed white-hot and could not be touched by mortal hands
Sang a war-song no other sword could match in volume
Drew sparks of red lightning from the forge wall itself
context: The sword was named Gram. Sigurd then tested it on the river by holding a wool-tuft against the current — Gram cut the wool cleanly as the water carried it past. With Gram he rode out to kill Fafnir on the moor where the dragon went each day to drink.

question: The Volsung hero Sigurd, riding the horse Grani that descended from Odin's own Sleipnir, came to the moor of the dragon Fafnir. Fafnir's hide was iron-hard above and on his flanks; only his belly was soft. An old man on the path (Odin in disguise) advised Sigurd to dig a pit on the track the dragon used each day to drink at the river, hide below, and strike upward. Sigurd dug pits and hid. Fafnir crawled overhead, the soft belly above the trench. Sigurd thrust the reforged sword Gram upward with both hands. What gushed down on Sigurd in the pit?
answer: The dragon's blood, soaking him from head to foot
choices: The dragon's blood, soaking him from head to foot
A torrent of coiled treasure-coin from the dragon's belly
The dragon's last breath, hot as a forge bellows
A swarm of dragon-flies that had nested in the wounds
context: Fafnir spoke before dying, warning Sigurd that the hoard was cursed — every owner was doomed to die over it. Sigurd refused to leave the gold. Some traditions say the dragon-blood that drenched him made him invulnerable except on a single spot between his shoulder-blades, where a leaf fell — the weakness through which his brother-in-law Guttorm later murdered him.

question: After killing the dragon Fafnir, the Volsung hero Sigurd cut out the dragon's heart at his foster-father Regin's instruction and set it to roast over a fire. Regin slept nearby. Testing whether the heart was cooked, Sigurd touched it with a fingertip, burned himself, and stuck the finger in his mouth. Fafnir's blood on his tongue gave him a sudden new ability. What was the first thing Sigurd heard the moment he understood the speech of birds?
answer: Two birds warning him that Regin meant to kill him in his sleep
choices: Two birds warning him that Regin meant to kill him in his sleep
Three birds singing the names of every god in Asgard
A raven of Odin commanding him to surrender the hoard
An eagle praising his deed and prophesying his death
context: Sigurd drew Gram and cut off Regin's head before the smith could rise. The birds also told him of a sleeping Valkyrie on a fire-ringed mountain to the south. He ate the dragon's heart, loaded Grani with cursed gold, and rode to find her. The whole episode is told in the Fafnismal of the Poetic Edda.

question: Following the birds' counsel after killing the dragon Fafnir, the Volsung hero Sigurd rode south on Grani until he came to a great mountain ringed in flames. He spurred Grani through the wall of fire and reached the peak. There he found a figure in full armor sleeping on a stone bier. He cut the corselet free with the sword Gram. The sleeper was a tall woman — a Valkyrie cursed by Odin with a sleep-thorn for defying his battle-orders. Who was she?
answer: Brunhild, who had given victory to the wrong king in defiance of Odin
choices: Brunhild, who had given victory to the wrong king in defiance of Odin
Gudrun, the king's daughter promised to him by fate from birth
Sigrun, who had loved a Norse hero from a rival royal house
Skuld, the youngest of the three Norns hidden by her sisters
context: Brunhild taught Sigurd runes and counsel before he rode on. They exchanged rings — Sigurd gave her the cursed Andvaranaut from Fafnir's hoard. They swore loyalty. The tragedy of their later separation (Sigurd magicked into forgetting her, marrying Gudrun, helping King Gunnar win Brunhild by deception) is the heart of the Volsunga Saga and Wagner's Ring cycle.

question: At the end of the war between the Aesir and the Vanir, the two divine families sealed peace by spitting together into a great cauldron. From the divine spittle the gods shaped a man — Kvasir, the wisest being in the nine worlds, who could answer any question put to him. He traveled widely teaching wisdom. Two cunning dwarfs named Fjalar and Galar invited him to a private feast at their hall, then murdered him. What did the dwarfs do with Kvasir's blood?
answer: Brewed it with honey into the Mead of Poetry in three vessels
choices: Brewed it with honey into the Mead of Poetry in three vessels
Poured it into a single jar and locked it in the Aesir's vault
Drank it themselves and gained the gift of every craft
Spilled it on their forge stone so the metal would sing
context: Any drinker of the Mead would become a poet or scholar. The two vats were called Son and Bodn; the kettle Odrerir. The dwarfs told the Aesir that Kvasir had choked on his own wisdom because no one was wise enough to ask the questions that would have saved him.

question: After brewing the Mead of Poetry from Kvasir's murdered blood mixed with honey, the dwarfs Fjalar and Galar tired of having no one to drink with. They invited a friendly giant named Gilling and his wife to visit. While she stayed in the hall, Fjalar took Gilling out in a small boat, rowed onto a half-tide rock, and drowned him. Returning to the hall the dwarfs told Gilling's wife the news. When she cried out in grief, what did Galar do?
answer: Dropped a heavy millstone on her head from the doorway above
choices: Dropped a heavy millstone on her head from the doorway above
Choked her with the rope they had used to bind Gilling
Crushed her between two iron doors as she ran out
Stabbed her with the same dagger that had killed Kvasir
context: Gilling's son Suttungr seized the dwarfs and rowed them out to the same tidal rock to drown them as they had drowned his father. They bought their lives by surrendering the entire Mead of Poetry. Suttungr locked the mead inside his mountain Hnitbjorg in Jotunheim and set his daughter Gunnlod as guard — the location Odin later raided in his Bolverkr disguise.

question: Determined to win the Mead of Poetry, Odin disguised himself as a wandering farmhand named Bolverkr. He worked Suttungr's brother Baugi for a summer, then asked as payment a single sip of his brother's mead. Baugi could not deliver but agreed to drill through the mountain Hnitbjorg with a magical auger called Rati. Once the hole was through, Odin took serpent-shape, slithered into the cave, and found Suttungr's daughter Gunnlod guarding three vats of mead. What did Odin do to win the three sips she granted him?
answer: Spent three nights with her, then drank all three vats in three swallows
choices: Spent three nights with her, then drank all three vats in three swallows
Sang three runic spells until she fell asleep at her watch
Promised her a place among the Aesir if she let him drink freely
Killed Gunnlod silently and drained the vats while she lay dead
context: Each swallow drained an entire vat. Odin then turned into an eagle and flew for Asgard. Suttungr saw him fleeing, took eagle-shape, and pursued. The gods set out vats in Asgard to catch the mead when Odin arrived. The story is told in the Havamal and Skaldskaparmal.

question: Returning to Asgard with the Mead of Poetry inside him in eagle-shape, Odin was pursued by the giant Suttungr also in eagle-form. The Aesir had set out three great vats in Asgard's courtyard to catch the mead. As Odin overflew them, with Suttungr closing fast behind, how did Odin deliver the mead to the waiting vessels?
answer: Spat it from his beak into the vats waiting below
choices: Spat it from his beak into the vats waiting below
Coughed it up in mid-flight and the gods caught it in nets
Vomited it into the vats and continued circling the city
Dropped a single golden feather containing all three vats' worth
context: Odin spat most of the mead cleanly into the vats. A small amount escaped backward as he flew — that scattered portion the Norse called 'the share of the poetasters,' the small mead anyone could find for bad verse. The vats became the source of true poetry, doled out from then on by Odin to those he favored.

question: The goddess Freyja owned a golden necklace called Brisingamen, forged by four dwarfs in exchange for an indecent price she had paid. Loki stole it from her sleeping chamber one night and fled with it across the sea. Heimdall, the watchman of the gods who could see for a hundred leagues and hear grass grow, spotted the theft from his post at the foot of the rainbow bridge. He pursued. Loki took seal-shape on the open water. What did Heimdall do?
answer: Took seal-shape himself and wrestled Loki on a skerry called Singasteinn
choices: Took seal-shape himself and wrestled Loki on a skerry called Singasteinn
Took eagle-shape and clawed the necklace from Loki's seal-jaws
Took whale-shape and rolled Loki onto the rocks of the shore
Stayed in his own form, riding the waves with his sword Hofund
context: Heimdall recovered Brisingamen and returned it to Freyja. The seal-fight is referenced in the 10th-century skald Ulfr Uggason's poem Husdrapa and preserved in the Prose Edda. Loki and Heimdall remain enemies through to Ragnarok — at which battle the two will kill each other.

question: The sea-giant Aegir held a great feast for the gods in his hall on Hlesey island, using the enormous cauldron Thor had taken from the giant Hymir. Servants brewed the ale; gold lit the hall instead of torches. Loki had been banished from the feast for killing one of Aegir's servants in jealous rage. He pushed back in anyway, demanding to be seated. The gods refused; he insulted them in turn. What god finally arrived and ended the flyting by raising Mjolnir over Loki's head?
answer: Thor, returning from an errand in the east
choices: Thor, returning from an errand in the east
Heimdall, blowing Gjallarhorn through the open door
Odin, casting Gungnir across the hall to pin Loki down
Tyr, drawing his sword and demanding single combat
context: The flyting is preserved in the Lokasenna of the Poetic Edda. Loki insulted every god and goddess in turn — accusing Odin of unmanly magic, Idunn of sleeping with her brother's murderer, Tyr of being unable to settle quarrels (cited as one-handed), Freyja of taking every Aesir to bed. Thor's arrival drove Loki out into the night. He fled to the waterfall hut where the gods caught him with the first fishing-net.

question: When the Aesir at last caught Loki for his role in Balder's death, they took him to a deep cave and brought in his two sons by the goddess Sigyn — Vali and Narfi. To bind Loki for eternity they used cords drawn from his own flesh-and-blood. First they performed a transformation on Vali. What did the gods do to him?
answer: Turned Vali into a wolf, and the wolf tore Narfi apart
choices: Turned Vali into a wolf, and the wolf tore Narfi apart
Sent Vali to Hel to swap places with his uncle Balder
Killed Vali first and used his entrails as the binding cord
Walled Vali alive inside the cave's stone behind his father
context: Narfi's entrails were then drawn out — and as the gods wound them around Loki across three sharp stones (shoulders, hips, knees) the gut-cords turned to iron. The giantess Skadi fastened a venomous serpent into the rocks above Loki's face. The Vali in this story is Loki's son — not to be confused with Odin's son Vali, born to avenge Balder.

question: After Loki was bound across three sharp stones with the iron-hardened entrails of his own son Narfi, the giantess Skadi placed a venomous serpent in the rocks above his face so that the venom would drip eternally into his eyes. Loki's faithful wife Sigyn refused to leave him. She stood beside her bound husband holding a wide bowl. Every so often the bowl filled and she had to turn aside to empty it. What did the Norse say happened during the moments when Loki's eyes were unprotected?
answer: The venom dripped, Loki convulsed in agony, and earthquakes shook the world
choices: The venom dripped, Loki convulsed in agony, and earthquakes shook the world
Loki cursed Sigyn, who fainted, and a fresh quake reset the cave
Lightning flashed across all nine worlds in answering pain
The snake fell silent and a long winter spread over Midgard
context: Loki's binding would last until Ragnarok, when his thrashing finally broke the cords and he led the giants against the gods. Sigyn's vigil with the bowl is one of the most-painted scenes in 19th-century Romantic Norse art (Brock 1893, Wahlbom 1855).

question: An anonymous builder came to the gates of Asgard and offered to wall the city against the jotnar in a single winter — completed by the first day of summer. In return he demanded three things: the goddess Freyja as bride, plus the sun, plus the moon. Loki, at the council, persuaded the wary gods to accept on the tight deadline he believed impossible. The builder asked one further condition that the gods reluctantly granted. What was the one further help the builder requested?
answer: The use of his stallion Svadilfari to haul stone at night
choices: The use of his stallion Svadilfari to haul stone at night
The right to recruit ten more giants of his choosing
Freyja's necklace Brisingamen as down-payment on his price
An iron tower built first as quarters for his work-camp
context: Svadilfari turned out to be a working wonder, hauling whole hillsides of stone every night. By three days from the deadline the wall was virtually complete. Loki was sent by the desperate gods to make sure the builder lost his bet — leading to Loki's transformation into a mare to lure Svadilfari away, and (months later) the birth of the eight-legged horse Sleipnir.

question: The gods loaded Balder's body onto his great ship Hringhorni, the largest in the nine worlds, to send him out to sea on a funeral pyre. Thor consecrated the pyre with a touch of Mjolnir. The giantess Hyrrokin came to launch the ship, which had been dragged onto rollers; she shoved so hard the rollers caught fire. At the very moment the burning ship was pushed onto the waves, what happened that made the gods weep doubly?
answer: Balder's wife Nanna died of grief on the spot and joined him on the pyre
choices: Balder's wife Nanna died of grief on the spot and joined him on the pyre
Mjolnir slipped from Thor's hand into the sea and could not be found
Odin's two ravens fell from his shoulders dead at the funeral fire
Balder's blind brother Hodr threw himself onto the burning pyre too
context: Nanna's body was placed on the pyre beside her husband. As Odin leaned down to whisper a secret word into the dead Balder's ear (a private message never recorded), he also placed his gold arm-ring Draupnir on the body as a parting gift. Both Balder and Nanna would remain in Hel until after Ragnarok, when the renewed world saw them return.

question: Loki, bored in Asgard, borrowed Freyja's cloak of falcon-feathers and flew east to Jotunheim to spy on the giants for sport. He perched on the window-ledge of the giant Geirrod's hall to look in. Geirrod, suspicious of a bird that stared too intently with too-human eyes, ordered a servant to bring it down. The servant scaled the wall and seized Loki by both feet. Geirrod looked into the falcon's eyes from close-up and recognized the trickster. He locked Loki in a small chest with no food for three months until Loki swore an oath. What oath did Geirrod force from Loki?
answer: To bring Thor to Geirrod's hall without Mjolnir, gauntlets, or belt
choices: To bring Thor to Geirrod's hall without Mjolnir, gauntlets, or belt
To deliver Freyja's necklace Brisingamen to Geirrod's daughters
To open the gates of Asgard at midnight on the next solstice
To bring Odin's spear Gungnir and his eight-legged horse Sleipnir
context: Loki swore the oath. Thor walked east stripped of his weapons. He stopped on the road at the cave of a friendly giantess named Grid (mother of the silent god Vidar), who lent him her own iron gauntlets, an iron belt, and a staff called Gridarvolr — the only reason Thor survived the trip.

question: Wading the river Vimur on the way to Geirrod's hall, leaning on Grid's iron staff Gridarvolr, Thor felt the water rise alarmingly under him — first to his thighs, then to his belly, then to his shoulders. Looking upstream he saw what was causing the flood. He shouted the proverb that gave the scene its name in Old Norse poetry. What was the cause of the rising water?
answer: Geirrod's daughter Gjalp astride the river, urinating into it
choices: Geirrod's daughter Gjalp astride the river, urinating into it
Geirrod himself, smashing a glacier into the river upstream
Two trolls felling oaks to dam the river above Thor
A great storm Geirrod had summoned with magical runes
context: Thor picked up a boulder from the riverbed and threw it at her with such force she fled. He shouted 'A river must be dammed at its source' — the line is preserved in the Thorsdrapa. He pulled himself ashore by gripping a rowan tree, which Norse legend therefore named 'Thor's rescue' (the rowan was sacred to Thor afterward).

question: Thor and Loki at last reached Geirrod's hall. Thor was led to the place of honor — a single low chair set against the back wall. As Thor sat down, he felt the chair lifting rapidly toward the rafters of the hall ceiling, which were studded with iron spikes to crush his skull. Bracing Grid's iron staff Gridarvolr above his head, Thor pushed the chair back down with all his strength. What was the result of the downward shove?
answer: He crushed Geirrod's two daughters Gjalp and Greip beneath the chair
choices: He crushed Geirrod's two daughters Gjalp and Greip beneath the chair
He shattered the iron rafters and they fell on Geirrod's head
He broke through the floor and dropped into the cave below
The chair shattered into splinters and Thor stood up unharmed
context: Both daughters' backs broke at once with a single sharp double crack. The same Gjalp had earlier tried to drown Thor in the river Vimur by urinating into it from above. Geirrod, hearing the cracks from his forge, stepped out with tongs gripping a glowing iron bar — preparing his third and final stratagem.

question: Hearing the crack of his daughters' backs breaking under Thor's seat, the giant Geirrod stepped out of his forge in the hall with a glowing iron bar gripped in tongs. He flung the molten iron across the hall at Thor. Wearing Grid's iron gauntlets, Thor caught the bar in mid-air and hurled it back. The iron passed through one thing after another in a single arc. What did the iron pass through?
answer: Geirrod, the pillar he had hidden behind, the hall wall, and the hill outside
choices: Geirrod, the pillar he had hidden behind, the hall wall, and the hill outside
Geirrod's hand and chest, two crossbeams, and the hall's iron door
The hearth-stone, the giant's throne, and the wall behind it
A wooden screen, Geirrod's shield, and his armored breastplate
context: The story is preserved in the Thorsdrapa by Eilif Godrunarson and in Snorri's Skaldskaparmal. Thor returned home alive thanks to Grid's three gifts — the gauntlets to catch the iron, the belt for the strength to hurl it back, and the staff to push the rising chair down. Loki had survived only by hiding behind Thor.

question: After Balder was killed by the mistletoe dart Loki tricked his blind brother Hodr into throwing, the gods of Asgard wept and mourned. Frigg asked who would ride down to Hel and beg for Balder's return. Hermod, one of Odin's sons, volunteered. What did Hermod borrow for the journey?
answer: Odin's eight-legged horse Sleipnir
choices: Odin's eight-legged horse Sleipnir
Freyja's chariot of cats and her falcon-cloak
Thor's iron-shod chariot pulled by the two goats
Heimdall's golden-maned stallion Gulltoppr
context: Hermod rode Sleipnir for nine nights down through dark valleys and across the river Gjoll on its golden bridge. He leaped the iron gate Helgrind in one bound — only Sleipnir among horses could have made that leap. Inside Hel he found Balder seated on a throne. Hel agreed to release him on one condition: every living thing in the nine worlds must weep for Balder.

question: Returning from Hel, Hermod brought back the terms — every living thing in the nine worlds must weep for Balder, and only then would Hel release him. The Aesir sent messengers through every land. All wept — stones, trees, beasts, men, even iron. Only one giantess in a cave refused. The Aesir later discovered who she really was. Who was the giantess Tokk?
answer: Loki himself, in giantess-disguise to keep Balder dead
choices: Loki himself, in giantess-disguise to keep Balder dead
Angrboda, mother of Loki's monstrous children Fenrir and Hel
Skadi, daughter of Thiazi, vengeful against the Aesir's hall
Hyrrokin, the giantess who had launched Balder's burning ship
context: Tokk was Loki himself in disguise. Because of this refusal Balder remained in Hel until after Ragnarok, when he would return to the renewed earth. The story is preserved in Snorri's Gylfaginning. The Aesir discovered the deception later and began the pursuit that ended in Loki's binding.

question: Loki, in one of his cruelest pranks, crept into Thor's hall while the goddess Sif slept and sheared off all of her famously beautiful golden hair, leaving her shorn to the scalp. When Sif woke and saw herself she wept; when Thor came in and learned what Loki had done, he seized the trickster by the throat. What did Thor threaten if Loki did not undo what he had done?
answer: To break every single bone in Loki's body
choices: To break every single bone in Loki's body
To hang Loki by his hair from Yggdrasil's branches
To bind Loki on the same three stones as later in legend
To turn Loki's own wife Sigyn against him forever
context: Loki swore he would replace Sif's hair with real spun gold from the dwarfs. He went to Svartalfheim and persuaded the sons of Ivaldi to forge the new hair, along with the spear Gungnir and the ship Skidbladnir — the first of six treasures from the wager-chain that eventually produced Mjolnir, Draupnir, and Gullinbursti.

question: After three nights with the giant Suttungr's daughter Gunnlod inside the mountain Hnitbjorg, Odin drained all three vats of the Mead of Poetry in three swallows. He took eagle-shape and flew for Asgard. Suttungr discovered the theft, took eagle-shape himself, and pursued with closing speed. The Aesir had set out three great vessels in Asgard's courtyard to catch the mead when Odin arrived. What did Suttungr the giant-eagle do with his closing wings as Odin overflew the walls?
answer: Burned them off on a fire the gods lit at the wall's top
choices: Burned them off on a fire the gods lit at the wall's top
Smashed them on the gates and tumbled stunned to earth
Folded them at Heimdall's horn-blast and dropped from the sky
Lost them when Thor's Mjolnir spun across to strike him
context: Suttungr fell inside Asgard's wall and was killed by the gods. The same fire-trick on the wall had earlier been used to burn the wings of the giant Thiazi pursuing Loki and Idunn — twice in the Eddas, the gods stop a giant-eagle by setting wood-shavings ablaze at the wall as he overflies it.

question: After Loki insulted every god and goddess at Aegir's feast and fled when Thor arrived with Mjolnir, he hid in a mountain hut above a waterfall, with four doors facing the four winds so he could watch every approach. To escape unseen if pursued, Loki took the shape of a salmon and dove into the pool beneath the falls. The Aesir, tracking him through Odin's high seat Hlidskjalf, came to the hut. They saw the burnt-out hearth where Loki had been weaving a fishing-net (he was the net's inventor). They copied the burnt pattern and wove the world's first replica. Who finally caught Loki as he leaped to clear the net?
answer: Thor, who grabbed the salmon by the tail
choices: Thor, who grabbed the salmon by the tail
Odin, who pinned the salmon to the rock with Gungnir
Heimdall, who scooped him out of the air with his sword
Tyr, who reached down and seized him from the shallow pool
context: Thor caught Loki so firmly that Loki's tail was elongated and narrowed in his hand — and the Norse said all salmon have had narrow tails ever since. With Loki captured the binding-of-Loki sequence began — the cave, the sons, the entrails, the snake.

question: The watchman of the gods, Heimdall, stood at the foot of the rainbow bridge Bifrost guarding Asgard against the approach of the jotnar. He could see for a hundred leagues by day or night and hear grass grow in a meadow or wool grow on a sheep's back. He needed less sleep than a bird. His parentage was unusual — the Eddas describe him as the son of nine mothers, all sisters. Who is named as the father of those nine mothers?
answer: Odin, the All-Father, in the lost Heimdallargaldr poem
choices: Odin, the All-Father, in the lost Heimdallargaldr poem
Aegir, the sea-giant who later hosted the Lokasenna feast
Bragi, the god of poetry and skaldcraft of the Aesir
Loki, in a story told before his treachery against Balder
context: The nine mothers are listed in the Heimdallargaldr (a fragmentary poem). They are sometimes identified with the nine waves of the sea — daughters of Aegir and Ran. Heimdall is depicted holding the great horn Gjallarhorn which he will blow at the dawn of Ragnarok. He and Loki are sworn enemies and will kill each other in the final battle.

question: At Aegir's feast in his hall on Hlesey, after Loki had insulted every god and goddess in turn through the long flyting preserved in the Lokasenna, Thor at last burst in from the east where he had been fighting trolls. Thor raised Mjolnir over Loki's head and demanded silence. Loki, even staring up at the hammer, threw back a final taunt. What did Thor warn Loki he would do next?
answer: Send Loki's head to Hel, ending his speech with one blow
choices: Send Loki's head to Hel, ending his speech with one blow
Stitch Loki's mouth shut with Brokkr's old thong of Vartari
Bind Loki with Vali's entrails on three sharp stones
Strike out Loki's eyes as Odin had once struck out his own
context: Loki replied that the threat was real and fled into the night. He hid in the waterfall hut as a salmon and was eventually caught with the world's first fishing-net. The Lokasenna preserves the entire flyting; the binding-of-Loki sequence followed after his capture. Thor's interruption is the only thing that ends a flyting of pure rhetorical violence in the Edda.

question: Thor walked north to the hall of the giant Hymir to fetch a brewing cauldron the gods needed for Aegir's feast. Hymir refused to give up the cauldron unless Thor broke a particular drinking-cup of his by sheer strength. Thor hurled the cup at a stone pillar — the pillar shattered, the cup did not. Then Hymir's wife (the giantess Tyr's mother in some versions) leaned over and whispered to Thor what he must throw the cup against. What did she suggest?
answer: The skull of Hymir himself, harder than any stone in the hall
choices: The skull of Hymir himself, harder than any stone in the hall
The iron anvil in Hymir's smithy out in the courtyard
The cliff Hymir's hall was carved into above the sea
The whetstone Odin had once cast aside and left on the floor
context: Thor flung the cup against Hymir's forehead. The cup shattered to powder; Hymir's brow was undamaged. Thor then heaved the great cauldron over his shoulder — the cauldron was a mile across in some versions — and walked out. Hymir and a host of giants pursued; Thor killed them all with Mjolnir on the road home. The cauldron passed to Aegir for the feast.

question: On the road outside the city after his contests at Utgard, Thor was overtaken by the giant-king Utgard-Loki, who confessed that every contest had been magical trickery — the horn had reached the sea; the cat had been the world-serpent; Elli had been old age; Thjalfi's racer Hugi had been thought; Logi had been wildfire. Furious at being deceived, Thor seized Mjolnir to strike the giant-king at last. What happened the instant Thor raised the hammer?
answer: Utgard-Loki and his whole city vanished, leaving Thor on an empty plain
choices: Utgard-Loki and his whole city vanished, leaving Thor on an empty plain
The giant-king laughed and stepped behind Mjolnir's swing unharmed
Mjolnir struck through Utgard-Loki and the blow had no effect at all
Heimdall blew Gjallarhorn and the giant-king turned to stone in shame
context: The Prose Edda warns that no second meeting with that giant-king has ever been recorded. The whole adventure — Skrymir's glove, the three blows, Logi the wildfire, Hugi the thought, the horn that was the sea, the cat that was the serpent, Elli the old age — is the longest single episode in Snorri Sturluson's Gylfaginning.

question: Riding to kill the dragon Fafnir on the moor where the beast drank each day, the Volsung hero Sigurd met an old gray-bearded man on the path. The old man (Odin in disguise, walking the world as he often did) studied Sigurd's plan. Sigurd was going to dig a single pit on the dragon's path and stab upward. The old man laughed and corrected him. What did the old man advise that saved Sigurd's life?
answer: Dig many pits, so the dragon's blood would not drown Sigurd in the trench
choices: Dig many pits, so the dragon's blood would not drown Sigurd in the trench
Stab into the dragon's eye instead, since the belly was armored too
Wait until Fafnir slept by the river before approaching at all
Bring three companions, since one man could not strike deep enough
context: Sigurd dug many pits as instructed. Fafnir's blood gushed down into the trenches above and around Sigurd, soaking him but not drowning him. Sigurd later understood the old man had been Odin himself, who took an active interest in the Volsung line. The whole arc is told in the Fafnismal of the Poetic Edda.

question: Traveling through Jotunheim with Odin and Hoenir, Loki and his two companions tried to roast an ox for supper. The fire would not cook the meat. An enormous eagle in a nearby tree called down — give me the best portion and your fire will cook. Loki angrily struck the eagle with the long pole on which the meat was hung. What happened to Loki when the pole touched the eagle?
answer: The pole stuck fast to the eagle and to Loki's hands at once
choices: The pole stuck fast to the eagle and to Loki's hands at once
The pole turned into a long snake biting his wrists
The pole sprouted into a small tree and pinned him to earth
The pole became a chain dragging him slowly into the fire
context: The eagle (Thiazi in disguise) flew off carrying Loki dangling at the end of the pole, dragging him through brambles and over crags until Loki begged for mercy. Thiazi demanded that Loki bring the goddess Idunn and her apples of youth out of Asgard as ransom. Loki agreed — and only afterward, with Freyja's falcon-cloak, undid what he had been forced to promise.

question: After Loki's mare-trick lured away the giant builder's stallion Svadilfari, the builder of Asgard's wall came up three days short of the deadline he had bet on. In rage at being cheated of his prize (Freyja, plus the sun and the moon), the builder threw off his disguise and revealed himself as a frost giant. The Aesir had sworn an oath of safe passage with the builder; killing him was a violation of that oath. Who returned just in time and did the killing anyway?
answer: Thor, returning from troll-hunting in the east, killed him with Mjolnir
choices: Thor, returning from troll-hunting in the east, killed him with Mjolnir
Tyr, who fought him hand to hand and threw him from the wall
Odin, who pinned him to the new stone with the spear Gungnir
Heimdall, whose horn-blast drove the giant fleeing to Jotunheim
context: The broken oath was an early sin of the Aesir, one of the events the Voluspa lists as foreshadowing Ragnarok — when promises sworn before gods break, the great cataclysm begins. The wall stood completed. Loki later returned to Asgard with an eight-legged foal named Sleipnir, the son of Svadilfari, which he gave to Odin as a gift.

question: After the Volsung hero Sigurd stabbed upward into the dragon Fafnir's heart with the reforged sword Gram, the dying dragon spoke at length from where he lay coiled across the river-track. Fafnir warned Sigurd that the gold he had won was cursed — every owner would be slain over it. Sigurd refused to leave it. The dragon also asked Sigurd's name and asked who his father was. Why did Sigurd answer indirectly at first, refusing his real name?
answer: Norse belief held a dying foe could lay a curse if he knew your name
choices: Norse belief held a dying foe could lay a curse if he knew your name
Sigurd was ashamed of his orphaned childhood with the dwarf Regin
His mother had forbidden him to ever name himself before strangers
He hoped the dragon would offer to spare him for a clever stranger
context: Sigurd at first called himself 'a noble beast' with no kin. Eventually he gave his real name. The cursed hoard, the Andvaranaut ring, and the dying dragon's prophecy are at the heart of the Volsunga Saga and reach down through the Nibelungenlied and Wagner's Ring cycle. Fafnir's warning came true: every owner of the gold was murdered, including Sigurd himself.
